summaries.text: An algorithm is a description of how to systematically perform a task, consisting of a sequence of steps. A program is a recipe for achieving a given task, written using a programming language.

A programming language describes the sequence of steps and allows for flexibility to pursue different sequences if something changes in between. A program can be executed by either a machine or a person, depending on the context.
The level of detail in describing an algorithm depends on the expertise of the group of people executing it, with more detail required for unfamiliar tasks.

An algorithm can compute numerical functions, such as calculating the square root of a number or X to the power of Y. It can also involve reorganizing information, like sorting a column in a spreadsheet.

Computations around us are often optimization problems, where information is rearranged to find the best solution. This includes travel booking sites finding the minimum time or cost flights, and computer programs like word processors suggesting spelling corrections.

The lecturer defines a program as something that manipulates information to a given requirement, not just a simple input-output process. The lecturer is introducing the concept of a data structure, which makes computations more tractable, and will illustrate this with an example of computing the greatest common divisor of two integers.

The lecturer is explaining that to find the greatest common divisor of two numbers, we look for the largest number that divides both, using the concept of a divisor. The lecturer is illustrating this with examples, including the numbers 8 and 12 where the GCD is 4, and the numbers 18 and 25 where the GCD is 1.
The GCD of any two numbers will always be well-defined because there is at least one common divisor, which is 1. To compute the GCD of two numbers, we will now outline a simple algorithmic procedure.

The procedure to compute GCD involves listing out all factors of two numbers, then finding the largest number common to both lists. The instructor questions whether this naive procedure constitutes an algorithm due to concerns over its finiteness and clarity.

The instructor identifies three clear steps that constitute the algorithm, and it is presented in a finite way. The process may take a different amount of time for different values of m and n, but the number of factors of m is always finite, between 1 and m.
To compute the factors of m, we test every number from 1 to m, checking if it divides m without a remainder. If it does, we add it to the list of factors.

The lecturer is now checking which numbers from 1 to 63 divide 63 without a remainder to find its factors. The first factors identified for 63 are 1 and 3, with the process ongoing to identify any other factors.

The lecturer is identifying more factors of 63, including 7, 9, and 21, and eliminating numbers that do not divide 63. The next step is to compare the factors of 63 with the factors of 14 to find the largest factor that appears in both lists.
The lecturer is systematically checking the factors of 14 to find the common factors with 63. The common factors found are 1 and 7, which are in ascending order as a result of the systematic check.

The lecturer is explaining how to write a detailed algorithm for finding the greatest common factor by systematically comparing the lists of factors for two numbers. The lecturer introduces variables to store the lists of factors, calling them "fm for m" and "fn for n".

The lecturer is now comparing the factors of m and n, adding any common factors to a new list called cf. The lecturer is then explaining that they will return the largest value from this list of common factors.

The lecturer is now explaining how to return the largest value from the list of common factors, which will be the rightmost value since they were added in ascending order. The lecturer is also noting that they have expanded the previous abstract algorithm into six more detailed steps, which can be used to write a Python program.

The Python program defines a function GCD of m, n, which takes two arguments m and n. It starts by computing the list of factors of m, which is done using a square bracket notation to represent an empty list.

The empty list of factors fm is assigned as the empty list. The code then enters a loop to check each value i from 1 to n to see if it is a factor of m, appending i to the list if m divided by i has a remainder of 0.
We are checking if i is a divisor of m, and if so, we append it to the right of the list fm. Now that we have computed fm for both m and n, we want to find the common factors between them.

We are creating a list cf of common factors by appending any factor from the first list that also appears in the second list. We then return the rightmost element of cf, which is the last common factor found.
The program returns the rightmost element of the list cf. This is achieved by using Python syntax, including colons and indentation, to make the code easier to read and understand.

We're noting key points from the set of Python steps: it requires names to keep track of intermediate values and some values can be single items. Intermediate values are tracked with names like m, n, i, j, and f.

Numbers such as i, j and f can be single values or collections like lists, which have a first position, middle element, and last position. These collections are called data structures, and one common type of data structure we'll be working with is the list.

We can explicitly assign a value to a name by using the equals sign, as seen in fn = [], which sets the value of fn to the empty list and tells Python that fn denotes a list. When we iterate over a list with a for loop, we are implicitly assigning each value to the corresponding name, as in for each f in cf.

The value of the name fn is being modified to take the old value and append a value to it, resulting in a new value. Assignment can either give a completely new value or update the old value using the current one.

We're not just executing a sequence of steps from start to finish, but rather doing some steps repeatedly and others only under specific conditions. For example, we might check every number from 1 to m if it divides m, and only append a number to the list of factors if it meets the condition of being a factor.

The lecturer will now explore the example in more detail, examining other ways of writing it and its features. This example is a good illustration of a program and will be looked at in further detail.
